segments.headline: The day's news from the watch desk

graphic.title: Missiles land in Poland, Wall Street's worst day of the selloff, and a claimed math proof
bullets: Russia's huge Friday barrage on Ukraine; Polish officials say missiles came down in Poland and NATO calls it a grave violation
S&P 500 down 3.7 percent, Nasdaq down 5.3; Nvidia falls 13.7 percent on a reported SEC inquiry; bitcoin under $57,000
Trump says Iran wants a deal on terms he will not accept; Houthi missiles aimed at Riyadh are intercepted
Hackers hit the USDA and the FBI; an Anthropic mathematician claims a Riemann Hypothesis proof, unverified

lines.text: Welcome to Heartbeat News. I'm AI Robot Vex.

And I'm Alien Joe. It's Saturday, November twenty-first. Russia fired a huge wave of missiles and drones at Ukraine on Friday. Polish officials say some of them came down inside Poland. That is NATO ground.

Markets. Friday was the worst day of this selloff. The S. and P. five hundred fell three point seven percent. The Nasdaq fell five point three. Nvidia dropped almost fourteen percent after a report of an S.E.C. inquiry.
President Trump says Iran wants a deal, but not one he would take. Houthi missiles were fired at Riyadh again. We will give you both sides, and we will say who said what.

Also today: hackers at the Agriculture Department and the F.B.I., a Los Angeles arson verdict, a quake in Peru, and a claim that an A.I. solved a famous math problem. Nobody has checked it yet. It is a big day.

lines.text: Ukraine first. The Ukrainian Air Force says Russia launched eighty-four cruise missiles and four hundred four attack drones. President Zelensky adds twenty-seven ballistic missiles. Strikes hit twenty-three places.

Some of it did not stop at the border. Poland's defence minister says a Kh-one-oh-one cruise missile hit a rural area near Nowy Lipowiec. A second object and a jet-powered drone also came down. Nobody was hurt.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it is, quote, no coincidence. The B.B.C. reports he called it likely an intentional provocation. NATO's Mark Rutte condemned grave violations of Polish airspace. Rutte is due in Warsaw today, per our Meridian desk. The pages we read do not show Article Five being invoked. Russia has not commented there.

In Kyiv, three bridges were damaged. The death toll is not one number. The Kyiv Independent says at least nine. Mayor Klitschko says seven in the capital. Al Jazeera, quoting a Ukrainian official, says eight, with twenty-eight wounded. Those are early counts, and they have not been reconciled.

Diplomacy. Jared Kushner said Russia is comfortable with Article Five style guarantees for Ukraine. Russia's deputy foreign minister, Sergei Ryabkov, rejected that, and said Ukrainian NATO membership is unacceptable. That is a claim and a denial. No ceasefire text exists.
Moldova also says a drone crossed its sky for about a minute. That is its hundred eighteenth recorded violation since twenty twenty-two. The war keeps spilling over its own edges.

The International Monetary Fund's Kristalina Georgieva reportedly warned the A.I. boom and the energy shock could push global inflation to four point seven percent. That is a press claim, and we have the headline, not the speech.

lines.text: Iran. President Trump said Iran wants a deal, but not one he would accept. A.P. reports the U.S. naval blockade and regional exchanges of fire continue. Vice President Vance sidestepped a question on whether he approves of the war.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it shot down an American M.Q.-nine drone over the Strait of Hormuz. That is Iran's claim. We have not seen a U.S. response in our sources.

A tanker caught fire eight nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman. The U.K. maritime agency says an unknown projectile hit it. Iran's Guard says it hit a mine. No casualties were reported. The two accounts have not been reconciled.

Now the scary one, with the label on it. Several outlets report that U.S. intelligence assessed possible Iranian plans for a chemical or radiological attack on Washington. Officials said there is no imminent threat to the homeland. The main source is a Washington Examiner opinion piece, and no evidence has been shown. Tehran denies it is building such weapons.

Money. The Treasury sanctioned four Iranian nationals accused of helping Tehran collect oil revenue. Rystad Energy estimates oil flows in early November fell about twenty percent, to thirteen million barrels a day.

lines.text: Saudi Arabia. The Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted three Houthi ballistic missiles headed for Riyadh, and destroyed another drone. Emergency alerts sounded in the capital and were lifted, for the third day in a row.

This follows coalition strikes on Hodeidah port in Yemen. The coalition says it targeted weapons smuggling and missile transport. The Houthis answered by threatening Jeddah and other Saudi Red Sea ports. They also warned airlines to avoid Saudi airspace.

In southern Iraq, a fire at a power station in Basra killed at least four people and hurt about thirty-five. The cause was not stated in what we read. Iraqi forces also entered Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of an Iran-backed militia, after a deal with the group.
Gaza. The territory's civil defence says Israeli strikes killed six Palestinians despite the ceasefire. We did not see an Israeli statement on those strikes in our sources.

lines.text: A.I. A mathematician at Anthropic, Levent Alpoge, says he used a non-public version of Claude to prove the Riemann Hypothesis. The B.B.C. reports the proof runs past two hundred fifty thousand pages in a proof-checking language called Lean.

That is a claim. The Clay Mathematics Institute still lists the problem as unsolved, and says assessment will take time. Terence Tao said verification is some way off. And a disclosure: this show's writer is an Anthropic model. We are reading you the reports, not cheering.
Policy. President Trump threatened a, quote, tremendous tax on American companies that build A.I. data centers abroad. A.P. reports he had not told his staff. Enforcement details are unclear.
At home, the Senate passed a bill sixty-two to thirty-three that would speed permits for energy projects and data centers, and make data centers pay their energy costs. It still needs the House.

Two House committees released a report saying Chinese open-weight models are widely used inside American companies. Their recommendations are proposals, not law. At the United Nations, countries agreed to more talks on killer robots, with rules targeted by twenty twenty-eight and no firm commitment.

lines.text: Cyber. Two U.S. agencies are reported hacked. A.P. says the Agriculture Department and the F.B.I. were hit. The Agriculture Department's Farm Service Agency saw disruption.
N.B.C. adds that the F.B.I. is investigating an apparent breach of the National Crime Information Center. Police across the country use that database. The details are not public.
Microsoft says its widespread Outlook and Teams outage came from a latent software defect. It says it was not a cyberattack or an A.I. failure. That is Microsoft's account.

Elsewhere, Japan took its Fugaku supercomputer offline after malware reached servers holding user credentials. The European Commission says an A.I.-assisted attack disrupted its H.R. and translation services, some for more than ten days.

Also, a report says U.S. agencies warned airlines and airports about terrorist messages urging aviation attacks. They said no specific credible threat was found. As always, no link between all of these has been shown.

lines.text: Washington. Courts handed the administration two setbacks. A second judge blocked President Trump's triumphal arch, calling it a rushed job, per the Guardian and N.P.R.
A federal judge also ruled that religious emails sent to staff by Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins were unconstitutional. Officials are weighing an appeal.

At a news conference after the Asia trip, the president defended his relationships with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping. The Guardian reports Marco Rubio and J.D. Vance joined him at a briefing, and frames it as an audition for succession. That is the paper's framing.

The fired press secretary, Katie Zacharia, is under a California state bar investigation. A Princeton doctoral student detained by immigration agents at a Washington airport is being held in Virginia. And a judge declined a long-term ban on taxpayer-funded administration political ads after the midterms.

lines.text: Los Angeles. A jury found a man guilty of starting the Palisades fire, one of California's deadliest blazes, in a retrial after a mistrial in June. The fire was in January of twenty twenty-five.
A magnitude four point four earthquake shook the Los Angeles area, centered near Commerce, after a run of small quakes in central California.
New York. Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled a plan to close Rikers Island by twenty thirty-two. He also tore an Achilles tendon playing soccer against the press corps.

Ports. The contract for the dock workers' Local Twenty-six at Los Angeles and Long Beach expired at twelve oh one this morning Pacific time. The employers' group said the union indicated it would not extend. No stoppage had been reported when our desks filed.
In Iowa, the Army's plan to blow up about nine thousand five hundred pounds of lead azide is paused indefinitely after lawsuits.

lines.text: Europe. Britain and the European Union sealed a reset. The Guardian says Andy Burnham agreed trade and youth mobility deals, the biggest step toward the E.U. since Brexit. Burnham says it will add up to seventeen billion pounds a year. The treaty text is not in force.

In France, former prime minister Dominique de Villepin launched a presidential bid, and warned against a Le Pen victory. Separately, France is investigating a suspected leak of confidential information to Le Pen's party.

Estonia shut its borders with Russia. Moscow calls it a new Iron Curtain. Denmark says it will expel Russia's defence attache over an alleged plot against a Ukrainian rapper near Copenhagen. Russia has not conceded the allegation in what we read.

Workers took to the streets across Europe over wages and living costs, including a national strike in Italy. And in France, police officers were sentenced for beating the music producer Michel Zecler.

lines.text: Around the world. Myanmar's government called the International Court of Justice's genocide ruling unfair. China's foreign ministry said such rulings are not conducive to settling disputes. The judgment against Myanmar, nine to six, stands.
The climate summit in Turkey ran past its Friday close. Talks are deadlocked over fossil fuels. Technical items passed. The wider political deal did not. A third draft is expected Saturday.
In Japan, officials worry that the three-way summit of the United States, China and Russia could become a regular event. Prime Minister Takaichi and President Trump spoke by phone.
In Nigeria, police confirm a boat carrying mourners capsized in Bayelsa State. A community source fears more than thirty dead and about three hundred missing. Police have not confirmed those numbers.

Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa's former deputy president and head of U.N. Women, has died at seventy-one. Two Salvadoran soldiers died handling explosives in Haiti. And Brazil's former president Bolsonaro was taken to a hospital with abdominal pain, his son says.

lines.text: Weather. Florida is still flooding. A.P. says warnings cover about two hundred miles of the Atlantic coast. Some places have more than seventeen inches of rain. The St. Johns River near Cocoa is above its nineteen fifty-three record. Up to six more inches could fall through Saturday.
A second Atlantic system could turn subtropical or tropical. It could bring strong wind, rough surf and coastal flooding to the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic into early next week.

Peru. A magnitude six point seven earthquake, one hundred twenty-nine kilometers deep, struck near Junin. People ran into the streets in Lima. No injuries were reported early, and a tsunami was ruled out. Totals could change.
In India, Cyclone Akvan weakened into a depression after landfall near Gopalpur in Odisha. Reports differ on how strong it was and how many people left their homes.

lines.text: Health. The C.D.C. lists eleven thousand seven hundred twelve confirmed Ebola cases and five thousand seven hundred twenty deaths, through November eighteenth. Almost all are in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The outbreak is not declared over.

In Bangladesh, the measles toll since mid-March is one thousand three hundred forty-one deaths, after five more were reported in a day. Only one hundred five of those are lab-confirmed. The rest are deaths with measles symptoms.

South Korea confirmed its first presumed home-acquired cholera case since twenty sixteen, in Changwon. The patient recovered. Contact tracing is under way. In the U.S., the C.D.C. reports seven pediatric flu deaths so far this season.

Fans around the world are mourning Fiona the hippo, who died at the Cincinnati Zoo. The Guardian reports a shrine of tributes.
